The Cutlib minnow Exoglossum maxillingua is a modestly sized cyprinid that occupies clear, fast-flowing streams throughout its range. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weigh approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], an initial mass reflecting the small size of the demersal eggs, which typically measure around 2 millimetres in diameter. These early developmental stages rely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-eclosion before transitioning to exogenous feeding. As the larvae grow through the pelagic phase, they gradually attain the size at which sexual maturation becomes possible. Based on length-frequency distributions of collected individuals, the total length at which puberty is reached has been established at 7.6 centimetres [Lp = 7.6 centimetres], a threshold that marks the onset of gametogenesis and the beginning of reproductive capability. This size at maturity appears consistent with that observed in other small-bodied leuciscine cyprinids sharing similar life-history strategies. At this same pubertal stage, individuals carry a wet weight of 4.65 grams [Wwp = 4.65 grams], reflecting the coordinated development of length and mass during sub-adult growth.

Once individuals surpass the pubertal size threshold, they undergo a period of rapid somatic growth that culminates in a maximum recorded adult mass. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully developed specimens in this population is 47.7 grams [Wwi = 47.7 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to the largest individuals captured in the system. Coinciding with this asymptotic mass, the corresponding total length for these mature adults reaches approximately 16 centimetres [Li = approximately 16 centimetres], with larger individuals occasionally exceeding this figure under particularly favourable resource conditions. This length marks the upper boundary of the species size distribution and is rarely surpassed even in older age classes. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a positive allometric pattern typical of fusiform stream fishes, with body condition indices varying seasonally in response to reproductive investment and prey availability. These metrics together define the upper limits of the species physical dimensions.

Reproductive output in Exoglossum maxillingua has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that closely mimic the thermal regime of its native habitat. At a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], spawning females deposit approximately 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 1 to 3 eggs per clutch], with individual females typically producing approximately 1.6 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.6 clutches annually]. The combination of moderate clutch sizes and a restricted breeding season results in a modest annual reproductive output, reflecting the species investment in comparatively large, nutrient-rich eggs rather than high fecundity. This spawning strategy aligns with that of other lithophilic spawners that deposit adhesive, demersal eggs in gravel substrates where parental guarding may occur. The incubation period lasts roughly 6 to 8 days at this temperature regime, after which free-swimming larvae emerge and begin their pelagic dispersal phase within the stream drift.

A detailed examination of body mass at key life-history transitions reveals distinct energetic thresholds that shape the species population dynamics. At the onset of reproductive maturity, individuals carry a wet weight at puberty of 4.65 grams [Wwp = 4.65 grams], a mass that corresponds closely to the pubertal length of 7.6 centimetres and indicates a coordinated developmental trajectory between linear growth and tissue accumulation. The roughly thousand-fold increase from the hatching mass of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] to the 4.65 gram pubertal mass is notable for a small-bodied leuciscine, reflecting the substantial growth required to reach reproductive size in swift, resource-variable streams. The mass gain from birth to puberty occurs over a period of several months, with growth rates modulated by seasonal temperature fluctuations and food availability. Juveniles that achieve this pubertal mass earlier in the growing season tend to have a longer window for their first spawning event, which may confer a fitness advantage in years with favourable hydrological conditions.

Longevity records for Exoglossum maxillingua indicate that individuals maintained at a consistent 18 °C [T = 18 °C] in captive rearing facilities can survive for up to 4 years [am = up to 4 years], a lifespan that is intermediate among North American leuciscine cyprinids of comparable body size. In natural stream environments, however, the realized lifespan is often shorter due to the cumulative costs of seasonal flooding and predation, and the intensity of spawning activity declines in the oldest age classes. These demographic parameters, when integrated with the growth and reproductive data, provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the population dynamics of this benthic-stream specialist.
